title: Documentation for Engineers
summary: READMEs, API contracts and runbooks that actually work when someone is stuck at 2am — plus the habits that keep them from rotting into confident, wrong instructions.

slides.markdown:
Picture your reader precisely: it is 02:14, they were paged, they have never touched your service, and they are three tabs deep looking for one command. Every documentation decision gets easier once that person is the target.

That reader does not want your architecture narrative. They want to know what this thing is in one line, how to run it, and what to do about the alert that woke them. If the answer is somewhere in your docs but takes eight minutes to find, you have failed the same as if you'd written nothing.

This topic is the practical documentation an engineer owns day to day: **READMEs**, **API contracts**, **runbooks**, and the two habits that keep them alive — **docs-as-code** and **explicit freshness signals**. It is deliberately not about design docs; those are [writing-design-docs](writing-design-docs).

slides.subTitle: It has users, and they arrive mid-task
slides.markdown:
Nobody reads documentation. People **search** documentation, mid-task, already frustrated. That single fact changes how you write it:

- **Optimise for landing in the middle.** Every section must make sense to someone who arrives via Ctrl-F and reads nothing above it. That means repeating a bit of context in each section instead of building a narrative.
- **Title by the task, not the subsystem.** `Rotating the Stripe webhook secret` gets found. `Webhook subsystem overview` does not — nobody searches for a noun they don't know exists.
- **Front-load the command.** The paragraph of caveats goes *after* the thing they came for, not before it.

A cheap measurement that beats any style guide: pick the five questions your team actually got asked in Slack last month, and time yourself finding each answer in your docs. Anything over 60 seconds is a broken page, and the Slack questions tell you exactly which pages to write next.

slides.sectionTitle: Four kinds of doc, one page each
slides.subTitle: Mixing them is why docs feel useless
slides.markdown:
Most bad documentation is not badly written — it is **four documents wearing one hat**. The Diátaxis split is the useful lens:

- **Tutorial** — get a newcomer to a first success. Linear, opinionated, no choices offered. "Run these six commands and see a green response."
- **How-to** — solve one specific task for someone who already has context. "How to add a new event consumer."
- **Reference** — exhaustive, lookup-shaped, boring on purpose. Endpoint tables, config keys, error codes.
- **Explanation** — the why. Trade-offs, history, mental model. This is where an [ADR](rfcs-and-technical-decision-records) link belongs.

The failure is a single `SETUP.md` that opens with a paragraph on the event-sourcing philosophy, drifts into an install walkthrough, and buries the config table at the bottom. The newcomer bounces off the philosophy; the expert can't find the table.

Split them, and each page gets short enough that people finish it.

slides.subTitle: The eight sections, in this order
slides.markdown:
A README's job is a cold start, not completeness. This order is deliberate — a stranger gets value from every section before they need the next:

```markdown
# orders-api
One line: what this is and who calls it.
"HTTP API that accepts customer orders and publishes order.created events."

## Status
Owner: #team-payments  |  On-call: payments-primary  |  Prod since 2024-06

## Quickstart              <- must work on a laptop, from clone, in <10 min
    make dev-up            # postgres + kafka in docker
    make seed
    curl localhost:8080/healthz

## Configuration           <- every env var: name, default, what breaks if wrong

## Running the tests
    make test              # unit, ~40s
    make test-integration  # needs docker, ~4 min

## Architecture (5 lines + link)
Orders -> Postgres (outbox table) -> poller -> Kafka. Details: docs/adr/

## Common tasks
Add an endpoint, add a migration, rotate the Stripe key -> docs/how-to/

## Troubleshooting
The three failures every newcomer hits, with the exact error text.

## Contributing
Branch naming, review expectations, how to release.
```

The **Troubleshooting** section is the one people skip and the one that saves the most time. Put the *literal error string* in it, because that is what the reader will paste into search.

slides.subTitle: The only README check that works
slides.markdown:
You cannot review your own README, because you already have the AWS profile, the `.env` file, and the tribal knowledge that the seed script must run twice.

So test it instead, with a real procedure:

1. Give it to someone who has never touched the repo — ideally a new hire in week one.
2. **Watch them, on a call, and say nothing.** This is the hard part and the entire value of the exercise.
3. Write down every place they stall. Each stall is a missing line.
4. They fix the README as their first PR. It is a genuinely useful first contribution and it captures the confusion before it fades.

What this surfaces, every single time: an undocumented prerequisite ("you need Docker 24+, 20 fails silently"), a step that only works if you're already VPN'd in, and a command that has quietly required an extra flag since March.

The automated version is a CI job that runs the Quickstart in a clean container on every merge. If your Quickstart is genuinely five commands, this is a ten-line workflow and it makes the README **impossible to silently break**.

slides.subTitle: Not parameter types
slides.markdown:
Generated parameter tables tell you what the compiler already knows. What callers actually need is the **contract**. Compare:

```text
BEFORE (a type dump)
  POST /v1/refunds
  charge_id  string   required   The charge id.
  amount     integer  optional   The amount.
  Returns: Refund object.

AFTER (a contract)
  POST /v1/refunds
  charge_id  string   required
      Must be a succeeded charge under 90 days old.
  amount     integer  optional  (default: full remaining amount)
      Minor units. Must be <= remaining refundable amount.

  Idempotency: send Idempotency-Key. Same key within 24h returns the
      original refund, and does NOT create a second one.
  Consistency: the refund is durable when we return 201, but the
      customer's bank may take 5-10 business days to show it.
  Errors:
      409 charge_already_refunded  - safe to treat as success
      422 charge_too_old           - not retryable, needs a manual credit
      429                          - retry with backoff, honour Retry-After
  Rate limit: 100 req/min per account.
```

Everything the AFTER version adds is something a caller would otherwise learn from an incident: whether a retry is safe, which errors are terminal, and what "done" actually means. Generate the type table from the schema; **hand-write the contract**, because no generator can infer it.

slides.subTitle: Copy-pasteable, with checks between steps
slides.markdown:
A runbook is written for a specific alert and read by a stressed, half-awake stranger. It is imperative, not descriptive:

```markdown
# Alert: OrderConsumerLagHigh
Severity: P2  |  Owner: #team-payments  |  Last tested: 2026-06-18 (game day)

## What this means
The order.created consumer is >5 min behind. Customers see "processing"
for too long. Payments are NOT lost - they are queued.

## Is it actually bad? (30 seconds)
    kubectl -n prod exec deploy/kafka-tools -- kafka-consumer-groups \
      --describe --group order-consumer
  If LAG is falling on its own -> it is recovering. Wait 10 min, do nothing.

## Step 1 - is the consumer alive?
    kubectl -n prod get pods -l app=order-consumer
  CrashLoopBackOff -> go to Step 3.  Running -> Step 2.

## Step 2 - is it a downstream stall?
    kubectl -n prod logs -l app=order-consumer --tail=100 | grep -i timeout
  Timeouts to fraud-svc -> page #team-fraud. Do not scale up; you will
  only add load to the thing that is already failing.

## Step 3 - scale out (safe, reversible)
    kubectl -n prod scale deploy/order-consumer --replicas=8
  Max 12: there are 12 partitions, extra pods sit idle.
  VERIFY: lag falling within 5 min. If not, escalate to payments-secondary.

## If none of this worked
Page @dan (principal). Do NOT purge the topic - it loses orders.
```

The non-obvious parts: an early **"is it actually bad?"** exit so you don't act on a self-healing blip, a **verification** after each action, and explicit **do-nots** for the destructive shortcut that looks tempting at 2am.

slides.subTitle: Confident instructions that no longer work
slides.markdown:
The dangerous runbook is not the missing one — it's the one written 18 months ago that reads authoritatively and is quietly wrong. The namespace was renamed, the script moved, the flag was deprecated. At 2am the on-call engineer trusts it, runs three commands that fail in confusing ways, and now spends the first 15 minutes of the incident debugging the runbook.

An untested runbook is worse than none, because none at least sends you straight to a human.

What makes them real:

- **Game days.** Deliberately trigger the failure in staging — or in prod, with the team watching — and have someone who did *not* write the runbook follow it verbatim. Every gap surfaces in one hour.
- **A `Last tested` date in the header**, not a `Last updated` one. Editing a typo doesn't prove a command still works.
- **Fix it during the incident.** The best moment to correct a runbook is while you're discovering it's wrong. A PR from the incident channel takes two minutes.
- **Let the postmortem write the next one.** Every recurring incident should exit with either a runbook or automation — see [postmortems-and-incident-learning](postmortems-and-incident-learning).

If a runbook's steps never vary, stop maintaining prose and turn it into a script. Documentation you can execute cannot drift.

slides.subTitle: Same repo, same PR, same CI
slides.markdown:
Docs-as-code means the docs are markdown files in the repo, changed in the same pull request as the code, and reviewed by the same reviewer. The mechanism is simple; the effect is that **the doc change becomes part of "done"** instead of a follow-up ticket nobody picks up.

What you get once docs live in git:

- **Review.** A reviewer who sees a new env var and no README line can block the PR — the same lever that keeps tests honest.
- **Blame and history.** `git log docs/runbooks/consumer-lag.md` shows who last touched it and why.
- **CI enforcement**, which is where the real teeth are: link-check every relative link so a moved file fails the build; run the README quickstart in a clean container; diff the OpenAPI spec against the handlers and fail on drift.
- **`CODEOWNERS` on `docs/`**, so doc changes route to the team that owns the system.

One rule makes it stick: **if a PR changes an interface, a config key or an operational step, it changes a doc in the same diff, or it explains in the description why not.** Codify that in the PR template and the review checklist rather than relying on discipline.

slides.sectionTitle: In the repo vs in the wiki
slides.subTitle: Staleness risk vs reach
slides.markdown:
Neither location wins outright — they fail differently, so split by what the doc describes.

| | In-repo markdown | Wiki / Confluence |
|---|---|---|
| **Updated with the code** | same PR, same review | separate task, usually skipped |
| **Versioned with a release** | yes — tag v2.1 has v2.1 docs | no, one live version |
| **Reviewable** | diffs, blame, CODEOWNERS | edits land unreviewed |
| **CI-checkable** | link-check, run the snippets | not really |
| **Findable by non-engineers** | poor — needs repo access | strong, one search box |
| **Good for** | READMEs, API contracts, runbooks, ADRs | org policy, onboarding, cross-team overviews |
| **Fails as** | invisible to anyone outside the repo | confidently stale after 12 months |

The deciding question is **"does this go wrong when the code changes?"** If yes, it belongs next to the code, where the same diff that breaks it can fix it. If it's about process or people rather than a codebase, the wiki is right and the staleness risk is lower anyway.

What you must not do is keep both. Two half-maintained copies means every reader finds the wrong one half the time. Pick one home per document and leave a one-line pointer at the other.

slides.subTitle: Let the reader calibrate trust
slides.markdown:
You cannot keep every doc current. You *can* tell the reader how much to trust each one, which is nearly as good and far cheaper.

A header block, on every operational page:

```text
Owner: #team-payments
Last reviewed: 2026-06-18 by dan@
Review by: 2026-12-18
Applies to: orders-api >= v2.4
```

Why each line earns its place:

- **Owner** as a team handle, never a person — people change teams, `#team-payments` doesn't.
- **Last reviewed** means "a human confirmed this is still true," which is a much stronger claim than **last updated** (someone fixed a typo). Only the first tells a 2am reader anything.
- **Applies to** stops the classic mismatch where the reader is on v3 and the doc describes v2.

Then automate the nagging: a weekly job that finds pages past their review date and opens a ticket for the owning team, or renders a **"this page has not been reviewed in 9 months"** banner at the top. A visible staleness banner is honest and takes seconds; silently rotting docs are how people learn to distrust all of them.

And when a doc is genuinely dead, **delete it.** A deleted page sends the reader to a human; a stale one sends them down a wrong path with confidence.

slides.subTitle: Every page is a maintenance liability
slides.markdown:
Each doc you write is something that can rot and mislead. Treat writing one as taking on debt, and only take it on where the code genuinely can't carry the information.

**Don't document — make the code say it:**

- Parameter types and required fields → the schema or type system already enforces this, and a hand-copied table drifts within a month.
- "How the retry loop works" step by step → a well-named function with a test called `test_gives_up_after_three_attempts` is the documentation, and it fails the build when it stops being true.
- Setup steps that are really a script → `make dev-up` beats fourteen numbered commands.

**Do document — the code cannot say it:**

- **Why**, including the alternative you rejected. Nothing in the source records the road not taken.
- **Contracts across a boundary** — idempotency, ordering guarantees, error retryability.
- **Operational judgement** — what's normal, what's alarming, what not to touch.
- **The surprising bits** — "this retry is deliberately not idempotent because the payment provider requires it."

The test: *could I make this fact self-enforcing instead of writing it down?* If yes, do that. Prose is the fallback for what you cannot encode.

slides.sectionTitle: Written by someone who already knows
slides.subTitle: The invisible missing step
slides.markdown:
The most common documentation defect isn't inaccuracy — it's the step the author couldn't see, because they'd done it so many times it stopped being a step.

The symptoms are always the same shape:

- **"Just deploy it."** Just how? Which pipeline? Does it need approval?
- **An unstated prerequisite.** The command works because the author is on the VPN, has `AWS_PROFILE` exported, and got added to a group six months ago.
- **The undocumented gotcha everyone knows.** "Oh yeah, you have to run the seed script twice, the first pass always fails." Every team has three of these and none of them are written down.
- **Vocabulary with no definition.** The doc says "run the reconciler" and never says what a reconciler is or where it lives.

You cannot self-review this, because the knowledge is invisible from the inside. The fixes are all external:

- **Watch a newcomer follow it in silence.** Every stall is a missing line.
- **Write down the question the moment it's asked in Slack**, in the doc, in the asker's words — those words are what the next person will search for.
- **Never say "just."** Whenever the word appears, a step is hiding behind it.

See [technical-writing-fundamentals](technical-writing-fundamentals) for the underlying habit: writing for the reader's context, not your own.
